deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text, only a pencil sketch. In the centre is a tetrahedron drawn in perspective, with one hidden edge dashed. Six lines radiate from it, roughly along three axes: one vertical (the upper half drawn as a thin elongated loop) and two oblique. On the upper-right ray sits a smaller sketch of the tetrahedron seen from that direction. It appears as a quadrilateral (square or rhombus) with crossing diagonals.

The page must be read with the previous one (p.19). There Grothendieck takes four points a, b, c, d and lists the three pairings Q_0 = (ad)(bc), Q_1 = (bd)(ac), Q_∞ = (cd)(ab). He writes the correspondence '(tétraèdre orienté + diagonale) ↔ (carré + codiagonale)' and the exact sequence 0 → V → S_4 → S_3 → 1. He then compares the Teichmüller and modular groups T_{0,4}, T'_{04}, T_{1,1} ≅ SL(2,Z) with S_4, S_3 ≅ SL(2,Z/2) and SL(2,Z/4)/±1.

This drawing is the geometric picture behind that correspondence:
- The three pairs of opposite edges of a tetrahedron on vertices {a,b,c,d} are exactly the three pairings Q_0, Q_1, Q_∞ of the four marked points of a genus-0 surface with four points. These correspond to the three cusps 0, 1, ∞ of M_{0,4}.
- Each pair of opposite edges defines a 2-fold axis through their midpoints, giving three axes and six half-axes (the six rays).
- Looking along such an axis, the tetrahedron projects to a square. The chosen pair of opposite edges becomes the two diagonals; the other four edges become the sides.
- So 'tetrahedron + a chosen pair of opposite edges (a diagonal)' corresponds to 'square + its two diagonals (codiagonal)'. That is what the small inset shows.
- The rotation group of the tetrahedron acts on the three axes, giving S_4 → S_3 (or A_4 → Z/3 for rotations). The kernel is the Klein group V of 180° rotations about the axes.

The sketch thus serves to visualise how S_4 acts on the four marked points of the (0,4) surface through S_3 on the three degenerations/cusps. It feeds into the computation of the extensions relating T_{0,4} and T_{1,1}.

ideas.what: The three pairs of opposite edges of a tetrahedron correspond to the three 2+2 partitions of four points, i.e. the three cusps/degenerations of M_{0,4}. The action gives S_4 → S_3 with kernel the Klein four-group.
ideas.modern_name: Exceptional surjection S_4 → S_3; tetrahedral symmetry and the 2-fold axes
ideas.where_published: Related themes (tetrahedral/octahedral dessins, M_{0,4}, T_{1,1}) appear in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), but not this specific sketch

ideas.what: Viewing a tetrahedron along the axis through midpoints of opposite edges gives a square whose diagonals are those edges ('tetrahedron + diagonal ↔ square + codiagonal').
ideas.modern_name: Orthogonal projection of the regular tetrahedron along a 2-fold axis

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a wordless illustrative sketch of classical tetrahedral symmetry. It supports the S_4 → S_3 and Klein-group computation on the previous page. There is no new mathematics here.
transcription_corrections: The transcription says 'six radiating lines'. More precisely they lie along roughly three axes (one vertical, two oblique). The upper vertical one is drawn as a thin elongated loop, consistent with the three 2-fold axes of the tetrahedron.

The 'smaller polyhedron drawn with diagonals' on the upper-right ray is best read as the tetrahedron seen along a 2-fold axis: a square or rhombus with both diagonals drawn. This matches 'carré + codiagonale' on p.19.
